metadata.title: Using convolutional neural networks to automatically score eight TIMSS 2019 graphical response items

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response item screenshots and human rater classifications as labels, then trains convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on image arrays. The paper describes stratified random splitting by country and score category and cross-validation, but it does not report applying TIMSS complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures. Because the task is automated scoring/classification of item responses (not estimating population achievement distributions), the authors’ ML pipeline appears to treat the response dataset as a modeling sample rather than a weighted survey for inference. The main preprocessing steps are image greyscaling, contrast/saturation adjustment, resizing to fixed dimensions, pixelation, and (for the trichotomous item) data augmentation to rebalance partial-credit representations.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not the dependent variable in this study: the targets are CNN classifications of item-level graphical responses into human rater score categories (incorrect/correct/partial/full), not cognitive achievement PV-based scores. Missing-data handling is not reported because the analysis is based on pre-extracted item response images and their corresponding human rater labels; the paper does not describe any imputation or deletion rules for missingness in predictors or labels. This omission is a reporting gap for transparency, even if missingness may be limited by the requirement that each response image and label be available for modeling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items only. From all graphical response items, selected eight items (five Grade 4 and three Grade 8; one Grade 8 item is trichotomous with partial credit) after excluding ME52048 (restricted use) from the von Davier et al. (2022) overlap and excluding one item at each grade due to lowest complexity. For each item, responses were collected from countries participating in eTIMSS 2019; then responses were split into training/validation sets using stratified random sampling by country and score category. Data cleaning removed responses that were (a) incorrectly scored by human raters or (b) inconsistently scored (“borderline”) across raters, based on manual review after CNN misclassification.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 4 Mathematics (Graphical response items; dichotomous scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: CNN classification of graphical responses (incorrect vs correct/partial)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best CNNs: average accuracy 99.37%–99.92% across seven dichotomous items; F1-scores between 0.9948 and 0.9992; average misclassified responses 11–99 (across items).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 4 Mathematics graphical response item the study leveraged convolutional neural networks to classify each student’s graphical response into the human rater score category, finding that the best models achieved near-ceiling agreement with human raters (average accuracy ~99.37%–99.92% and F1 ~0.9948–0.9992). This indicates that CNN-based automated scoring can reliably serve as a second scoring channel for graphical CR items, potentially reducing the need for additional human raters while maintaining scoring consistency.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 Mathematics (Graphical response items; trichotomous scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: CNN classification of graphical responses (incorrect vs partial vs full credit)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Trichotomous item ME62300: accuracy 97.99% and average F1-score 0.9766 on the clean validation sample; misclassified 233 responses on average; on incorrectly human-scored responses, correct classification accuracy 88.81% with 202 correctly classified out of 227.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 Mathematics graphical response item the study leveraged convolutional neural networks to classify each student’s response into incorrect/partial/full categories, finding that performance remained high but lower than dichotomous items (accuracy ~97.99% and F1 ~0.9766 for ME62300). This indicates that CNN-based validation is feasible for more complex graphical items with partial-credit categories, but operational deployment may require additional attention to class imbalance and borderline/partial-credit distinctions.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether convolutional neural networks can automatically score TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items by matching CNN classifications to human rater score categories. The authors selected eight graphical items (five Grade 4 and three Grade 8, including one trichotomous partial-credit item) and trained CNNs on preprocessed student response images (greyscale conversion, contrast/saturation adjustment, resizing to fixed dimensions, and pixelation; plus augmentation for the trichotomous item). Performance was assessed using hold-out validation and five cross-validation splits, reporting exact match accuracy, loss, and F1-scores to address class imbalance. Across seven dichotomous items, best models achieved average accuracy ~99.37%–99.92% with F1 ~0.9948–0.9992, and for the trichotomous item ME62300 accuracy was ~97.99% with F1 ~0.9766. The paper does not report applying TIMSS survey weights and provides limited transparency on missing-data handling, so results primarily support scoring reliability rather than population-representative inference.
